messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] is this paper at related to the No U-Turn concept in NUTS
parts:
Nope, the two algorithms are fundamentally different on a variety of levels. The paper you introduce is measuring curvature at various scales for classification, appeals to the Frenet-Serret formulas which are valid only in 2 and 3 dimensions, etc whereas NUTS is specific to Markov Chain Monte Carlo. In particular, NUTS is a specific application of Neal's "ensemble MCMC" approach (http://arxiv.org/abs/1101.0387).

Here's what's going on. What we want to be able to do is terminate trajectories when they "turn around", as any motion after the turning point reduces the distance between the initial point and the proposal, increases autocorrelations, and wastes computation. Unfortunately we can't apply any termination criterion to a HMC trajectory without breaking detailed balance. NUTS gets around this by introducing an intermediate ensemble, initial point -> binary tree -> proposal point, that preserves the target distribution. If we use our previous termination criterion on every subtree within the intermediate binary tree, then the building of the tree terminates approximately at the turning point we desired above but without breaking detailed balance.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] is this paper at related to the No U-Turn concept in NUTS
parts:
I don't think anyone immediately grasps NUTS -- it certainly took me a loooooooong time to fully understand it. I would recommend first making sure you understand how "windows" work in HMC (Radford discusses them in his HMC paper, but his ensemble paper goes into more depth). With windows you have a transition initial point -> window -> proposed point that nicely parallels NUTS. If you can prove that windows preserve the target distribution then it's pretty easy to show that a tree of specific depth (or a random depth) does so as well.

Once you have that, you'll need to convince yourself why a termination criterion on HMC breaks detailed balance (just keep reversing everything -- there's no reason why an arbitrary initial point would satisfy the termination criterion when simulating backwards from the final point). Lastly, how does the binary tree get around this? Admittedly, this is the hardest part.

If any of the individual steps trip you up let me know -- in order to convince myself I've written a bunch of scattered LaTeX notes that might be of help.
